question_text: A municipal assembly passes a by-law that directly contradicts a provision of the Constitution. According to the Constitution, what happens to that by-law?
option_a: It remains fully valid until the Supreme Court reviews every by-law.
option_b: It is void to the extent of its inconsistency with the Constitution.
option_c: It automatically amends the Constitution.
option_d: It stands because the majority of the assembly voted for it.
explanation: Article 1 (1): 'This Constitution is the fundamental law of Nepal. Any law inconsistent with this Constitution shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.'

question_text: At a debate, a speaker claims that all state power should belong to the elected cabinet rather than to the people. Under the Constitution, in whom is the sovereignty and state authority of Nepal vested?
option_a: In the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers
option_b: In the Federal Parliament
option_c: In the Nepalese people
option_d: In the Supreme Court
explanation: Article 2 (1): 'The sovereignty and state authority of Nepal shall be vested in the Nepalese people. It shall be exercised in accordance with the provisions set forth in this Constitution.'

question_text: A student argues that only Nepali-speaking citizens form the Nepalese nation. Which description of the nation matches the Constitution?
option_a: Only citizens who speak the official language
option_b: Only people living in the federal districts
option_c: Everyone who holds a Nepali passport, wherever they live
option_d: All Nepalese people across ethnicities, languages, religions, cultures and geographical diversities, united by allegiance to national independence, territorial integrity, national interest and prosperity
explanation: Article 3 (1): 'All the Nepalese people, with multiethnic, multilingual, multi-religious, multicultural characteristics and in geographical diversities, and having common aspirations and being united by a bond of allegiance to national independence, territorial integrity, national interest and prosperity of Nepal, collectively constitute the nation.'

question_text: A pundit suggests Nepal should sell a portion of its border territory to settle foreign debt. What does the Constitution say about Nepal's status?
option_a: Nepal is an independent, indivisible, sovereign, secular, inclusive, democratic, socialism-oriented, federal democratic republican state
option_b: Nepal is a secular republic that may cede territory by a two-thirds vote of Parliament
option_c: Nepal is a federal state whose provinces may transfer territory with their consent
option_d: Nepal is an independent kingdom; territory changes need only royal approval
explanation: Article 4 (1): 'Nepal is an independent, indivisible, sovereign, secular, inclusive, democratic, socialism-oriented, federal democratic republican state.'

question_text: A border official is caught leaking security maps to a foreign agent for money. Under the Constitution, what happens to conduct that is contrary to the national interest?
option_a: It is tolerated as a private matter between the official and the agent
option_b: It is punishable by Federal law
option_c: It is governed only by the laws of the concerned State
option_d: It becomes legal if the official apologises and returns the money
explanation: Article 5 (2): 'Any conduct and act contrary to the national interest shall be punishable by the Federal law.' Article 5 (1) lists freedom, sovereignty, territorial integrity, nationality, independence and dignity of Nepal, the rights of the Nepalese people, border security and economic wellbeing and prosperity as the basic elements of national interest.

question_text: Which statement about the languages of Nepal matches the Constitution?
option_a: Only Nepali is a language of the nation
option_b: All languages spoken as mother tongues in Nepal are languages of the nation
option_c: Only languages with an established written literature count
option_d: Only the languages used in official government work count
explanation: Article 6 (1): 'All languages spoken as the mother tongues in Nepal are the languages of the nation.' This is about recognition, not official use (official language is governed by Article 7).

question_text: A Province whose residents largely speak Maithili wants to use Maithili in its official work in addition to Nepali. What does the Constitution allow?
option_a: Nothing - only the Nepali language in Devnagari script may be used officially anywhere
option_b: The Province may, by a State law, determine one or more languages of the nation spoken by a majority within the State as its additional official language(s)
option_c: The Language Commission alone may declare official languages without any law
option_d: Only the Federal Parliament may choose a Province's official languages
explanation: Article 7 (1) makes Nepali in the Devnagari script the official language. Article 7 (2) lets a State determine, by a State law, one or more languages of the nation spoken by a majority within the State as additional official language(s).

question_text: You are designing a poster of the national flag. Which shape and design matches the Constitutional description?
option_a: Two juxtaposed triangular figures with a crimson-coloured base and deep blue borders, a white crescent moon with eight visible rays above and a white twelve-rayed sun below
option_b: A single rectangular crimson banner with a deep blue border and a white star in the centre
option_c: A triangular crimson flag with a white lion emblem and olive branches
option_d: A round crimson emblem with a white bird and gold border
explanation: Article 8 (1): 'The national flag of Nepal consists of two juxtaposed triangular figures with a crimson-coloured base and deep blue borders, there being a white emblem of the crescent moon with eight rays visible out of sixteen in the upper part and a white emblem of a twelve rayed sun in the lower part.'

question_text: A school textbook lists Nepal's national symbols. Which line is correct according to the Constitution?
option_a: National flower - Rhododendron Arboreum; national colour - crimson; national animal - Cow; national bird - Lophophorus
option_b: National flower - Orchid; national colour - saffron; national animal - Elephant; national bird - Peacock
option_c: National flower - Lotus; national colour - white; national animal - Tiger; national bird - Eagle
option_d: National flower - Marigold; national colour - green; national animal - Yak; national bird - Sparrow
explanation: Article 9 (3): 'The Rhododendron Arboreum shall be the national flower, Crimson Colour shall be the national colour, the Cow shall be the national animal and the Lophophorus shall be the national bird of Nepal.'

question_text: After living and working abroad for many years, a Nepali citizen returns home and is told by an official that he has lost his right to citizenship because of the long stay overseas. What does the Constitution say about this?
option_a: No citizen of Nepal may be deprived of the right to obtain citizenship
option_b: The right is lost automatically after ten continuous years abroad
option_c: The right lapses and can only be restored by paying a fine
option_d: Citizenship ends once a person takes up residence in another country
explanation: Article 10 (1): 'No citizen of Nepal may be deprived of the right to obtain citizenship.' Article 10 (2) adds that there is a single federal citizenship with State identity in Nepal.

question_text: Anjali, a Nepali citizen by descent, is married to a French citizen. Their daughter Sita was born in Nepal, permanently resides there and has never acquired any foreign citizenship. How can Sita obtain Nepali citizenship?
option_a: Not at all - a child of a foreign father can never be a citizen
option_b: She may acquire naturalized citizenship, since she was born to a Nepali mother, has permanently resided in Nepal and has not acquired a foreign citizenship
option_c: Only after both parents obtain a court order approving her citizenship
option_d: Only by being granted honorary citizenship by the Government of Nepal
explanation: Article 11 (7): in the case of a person born from a woman who is a citizen of Nepal and married to a foreign citizen, the person may acquire the naturalized citizenship of Nepal in accordance with the Federal law if he or she has permanently resided in Nepal and has not acquired the citizenship of a foreign country.

question_text: Elena, a foreign national, marries a Nepali citizen. Which statement about her citizenship matches the Constitution?
option_a: She automatically becomes a citizen on the day of the wedding
option_b: She may, if she so wishes, acquire the naturalized citizenship of Nepal as provided for in the Federal law
option_c: She must wait twenty years before she may apply
option_d: She can never become a citizen while she remains married
explanation: Article 11 (6): 'A foreign woman who has a matrimonial relationship with a citizen of Nepal may, if she so wishes, acquire the naturalized citizenship of Nepal as provided for in the Federal law.'

question_text: A newborn is found abandoned in Kathmandu and nobody knows who the parents are. What does the Constitution provide until the parents are traced?
option_a: The child is stateless and entrusted to the care of the State
option_b: The child is a citizen of Nepal by descent until the father or mother of the child is traced
option_c: The child may apply for citizenship only upon attaining majority
option_d: Citizenship depends on the district in which the child was found
explanation: Article 11 (4): 'Every minor who is found within Nepal and the whereabouts of whose father and mother are not known shall, until the father or the mother of the child is traced, be a citizen of Nepal by descent.'

question_text: After receiving citizenship by descent, Prakash wants his certificate to record his mother's name for gender identity. What does the Constitution allow?
option_a: A descent citizen may obtain a certificate of citizenship with gender identity in the name of his or her mother or father
option_b: Only the father's name may appear on a citizenship certificate
option_c: Adding gender identity to a certificate requires a court order
option_d: A person must take citizenship from one parent only and can never change the record
explanation: Article 12 (1): a person who obtains citizenship by descent may obtain a certificate of citizenship with gender identity by the name of his or her mother or father.

question_text: A citizen asks how the acquisition, reacquisition and termination of citizenship are regulated. What does the Constitution say?
option_a: These matters are decided case-by-case by the district administration
option_b: They are as provided for in the Federal law
option_c: They are governed by the customary law of each State
option_d: Citizenship, once acquired, can never be reacquired or terminated
explanation: Article 13 (1): 'Other matters relating to the acquisition, reacquisition and termination of citizenship shall be as provided for in the Federal law.'

question_text: Ramesh was born in Nepal, later settled in the United States and took American citizenship; his father had been a Nepali citizen by descent. Which of the following applies under the Constitution?
option_a: He loses all connection with Nepal and can never regain any form of Nepali citizenship
option_b: He may be granted non-resident Nepali citizenship entitling him to economic, social and cultural rights per the Federal law, as he resides outside a SAARC member state
option_c: He automatically resumes Nepali citizenship simply by submitting a letter
option_d: He can only be considered if he renounces his US passport immediately
explanation: Article 14 (1) allows non-resident citizenship to a person who has acquired a foreign citizenship, resides outside a SAARC member state, and whose parent or grandparent was previously a Nepali citizen by descent or birth; the holder may enjoy economic, social and cultural rights in accordance with the Federal law.

question_text: Which statement about citizenship records matches the Constitution?
option_a: Every citizen must keep a paper registry maintained by the ward office
option_b: The maintenance of records setting out the identity of every citizen is as provided for in the Federal law
option_c: Citizenship records are maintained by foreign embassies
option_d: The Constitution requires no record-keeping at all
explanation: Article 15 (1): 'Other matters relating to the maintenance of records setting out the identity of every citizen of Nepal and the citizenship of Nepal shall be as provided for in the Federal law.'

question_text: After a spate of violent crimes, a legislator proposes a draft law reintroducing the death penalty for murder. Under the Constitution, what is the position?
option_a: The death penalty may be imposed where the crime is proved beyond reasonable doubt
option_b: No law may be made providing for the death penalty, because every person has the right to live with dignity
option_c: The death penalty is permitted only with the approval of a majority of provincial assemblies
option_d: The death penalty is allowed if an ordinance is issued first
explanation: Article 16 (2) is categorical: 'No law shall be made providing for the death penalty to any one,' read with the right of every person to live with dignity in clause (1).

question_text: Suman distributes leaflets peacefully in a public square, but police detain him and hold him overnight without any legal basis. Which provision is most directly engaged?
option_a: No person shall be deprived of his or her personal liberty except in accordance with law
option_b: The police may detain anyone who appears suspicious without any order
option_c: Personal liberty may be restricted whenever an officer deems it necessary
option_d: Citizens may only assemble if a magistrate personally attends
explanation: Article 17 (1) protects personal liberty: 'No person shall be deprived of his or her personal liberty except in accordance with law,' and clause (2) guarantees every citizen freedoms including peaceful assembly.

question_text: After their father dies, a family divides the ancestral land, giving the son twice the daughter's share on the ground that he is male. The daughter objects. Under the Constitution, this is:
option_a: Permitted if the son agrees to maintain the daughter
option_b: Permitted where the father expressed such a wish in his will
option_c: Prohibited, because all offspring have an equal right to ancestral property without discrimination on the ground of gender
option_d: Permitted under customary practice recognised by a village gathering
explanation: Article 18 (5): 'All offspring shall have the equal right to the ancestral property without discrimination on the ground of gender,' alongside equal protection of the law in clause (1).

question_text: A district office orders a news website to pull an article criticising a government programme, saying it will otherwise seal the office and seize its computers. Which statement is correct?
option_a: The office may censor or seal any publication it dislikes
option_b: No news item may be censored, and no press or means of communication may be closed, seized or interrupted except in accordance with law
option_c: Censorship is allowed for anything the Government does not endorse
option_d: Only online media can be restricted without a court order
explanation: Article 19 (1) bars censorship of news items and other material, and clause (3) provides that no means of communication including the press, electronic broadcasting and telephone shall be interrupted except in accordance with law.

question_text: Police arrest Bikash on a Friday evening and produce him before the relevant judicial authority on the following Monday afternoon, three full days later, with no distance-related delay. How does this measure up to the Constitution?
option_a: It is valid because suspects may be held over weekends
option_b: It is valid if his family was informed the next day
option_c: It violates his rights: a person arrested must be produced before the adjudicating authority within twenty-four hours, excluding journey time
option_d: It is valid whenever an investigation is still ongoing
explanation: Article 20 (3) requires production before the adjudicating authority within twenty-four hours of arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey, and clause (1) requires the ground of arrest to be stated.

question_text: Anita, a victim of a burglary, asks the investigating police for the status of the investigation and proceedings. The officer refuses, telling her it is none of her business. The Constitution provides that:
option_a: A victim has no right to information once the complaint is lodged
option_b: A victim of crime has the right to get information about the investigation and proceedings of the case, and the right to justice including social rehabilitation and compensation
option_c: Only the accused enjoys procedural rights
option_d: Information may only be given through a lawyer engaged by the State
explanation: Article 21 (1) gives the victim of crime a right to information about the investigation and proceedings of the case in which he or she is the victim, and clause (2) guarantees justice including social rehabilitation and compensation.

question_text: A detainee is beaten at a police station to force a confession and is later freed without any action. Under the Constitution and law, which statement is correct?
option_a: Such treatment is punishable by law and the victim has the right to obtain compensation
option_b: The conduct is unlawful but no compensation may ever be claimed
option_c: It is permitted whenever a suspect is 'difficult'
option_d: Only physical, not mental, pressure on a detainee is prohibited
explanation: Article 22 (1) prohibits subjecting an arrested or detained person to physical or mental torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; clause (2) makes any such act punishable by law and grants the victim a right to compensation.

question_text: Authorities hold a journalist under preventive detention for suggesting the Government in a private chat might stall road building, and do not inform her family. Which of the following is correct?
option_a: Preventive detention is valid so long as an officer believes it prudent
option_b: Preventive detention may be imposed only where there is a sufficient ground of an immediate threat to the sovereignty, territorial integrity or public peace and order of Nepal, and the family must be informed immediately
option_c: Family members are never informed until release
option_d: Preventive detention may last indefinitely without any review
explanation: Article 23 (1) confines preventive detention to a sufficient ground of an immediate threat to sovereignty, territorial integrity or public peace and order; clause (2) requires information to be given to family members immediately; clause (3) entitles a person detained contrary to law or in bad faith to compensation.

question_text: At a village shop, a customer of a particular caste is told she cannot dine from the same utensils as others, and a co-manager later discriminates against a Dalit worker in the workplace. Which statement is correct?
option_a: Untouchability in private premises is acceptable as long as it is 'traditional'
option_b: No form of untouchability or discrimination is allowed in public or private places, workplace discrimination is prohibited, and such conduct is a severe social offence punishable by law with compensation for the victim
option_c: Only public places are protected; private homes and shops are exempt
option_d: Workplace matters are governed solely by the employer's discretion
explanation: Article 24 (1) prohibits untouchability in any form in private and public places; clause (4) bars workplace discrimination; clause (5) makes such acts a severe social offence punishable by law, with compensation for the victim.

question_text: The State requisitions a farmer's land to build a private amusement park, offering no compensation and saying it will decide the 'basis' later by internal order. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Property may be requisitioned only for public interest, and the basis of compensation and procedures must be as provided for in an Act
option_b: The State may take any property without any compensation
option_c: Only agricultural land is shielded from requisition
option_d: Compensation is payable only if the owner objects within seven days
explanation: Article 25 (2) allows requisition or encumbrance on property only for public interest, and clause (3) provides that the basis of compensation and the procedures to be followed shall be as provided for in the Act.

question_text: An organisation sets up camps that pressure people into leaving their religion through offers of cash and gifts organised by one denomination. Under the Constitution, this is:
option_a: Lawful, because everyone is free to promote their own faith aggressively
option_b: Unlawful only if physical force is used
option_c: Contrary to the Constitution, because no person shall convert or cause the conversion of another person from one religion to another, and the right may not be exercised contrary to public peace and decency
option_d: Lawful if the target community approves by a majority
explanation: Article 26 (1) protects the freedom to profess, practise and protect one's religion; clause (3) expressly forbids such acts as converting another person from one religion to another or acts contrary to public health, decency, morality or peace.

question_text: A citizen files a formal request for audit details of a public mega-project, but the office refuses, citing 'routine policy preference' while pointing to no law on confidentiality. Under the Constitution:
option_a: He has no right to such information
option_b: Every citizen has the right to demand and receive information of interest or of public interest, and confidentiality can be maintained only where provided for in accordance with law
option_c: Information may be withheld at the discretion of the concerned minister
option_d: Requests must be renewed monthly before any reply
explanation: Article 27 (1) confers on every citizen the right to demand and receive information on any matter of his or her interest or of public interest, subject only to confidentiality that must be maintained in accordance with law.

question_text: A clinic publishes a patient's medical records on its website to advertise services, without consent or any legal basis. Under the Constitution, the patient's position is that:
option_a: Medical records are not protected once a patient is discharged
option_b: The privacy of a person, including data and documents, is inviolable except in accordance with law
option_c: Consent is required only for photographs, not written records
option_d: Publishing is allowed if the names are partially masked
explanation: Article 28 (1): 'The privacy of any person, his or her residence, property, document, data, correspondence and matters relating to his or her character shall, except in accordance with law, be inviolable.'

question_text: An agent lures a young woman abroad for a 'hotel job', confining her and taking her earnings once there. Back in Nepal, she brings a claim. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Trafficking and holding a person in slavery or servitude are prohibited, and the victim may obtain compensation from the perpetrator
option_b: The prohibition covers only children
option_c: No one may be punished if the person 'voluntarily' accepted the arrangement
option_d: Compensation is possible only if the victim was a citizen at the time
explanation: Article 29 (3) prohibits trafficking, slavery and servitude; clause (4) prohibits forcing anyone to work against his or her will; clause (5) makes such acts punishable by law and grants the victim the right to compensation from the perpetrator.

question_text: A tannery upstream releases untreated waste into the river, and downstream villagers fall sick. Under the Constitution, the villagers:
option_a: Have no remedy because pollution is a matter for local custom
option_b: Have the right to obtain compensation, in accordance with law, for injury caused by environmental pollution or degradation, as part of the right to live in a clean and healthy environment
option_c: May only complain to the polluter, who may refuse to respond
option_d: Must first plant compensatory trees before any claim
explanation: Article 30 (1) guarantees every citizen the right to live in a clean and healthy environment; clause (2) gives the victim the right to compensation for injury caused by environmental pollution or degradation.

question_text: A school in a remote municipality demands a tuition fee from students at the secondary level and refuses admission to a child whose family cannot pay. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Secondary education may be fee-based at a school's discretion
option_b: Every citizen has the right to compulsory and free education up to the basic level and free education up to the secondary level from the State
option_c: Fees are lawful if kept below a monthly threshold
option_d: Schools may charge whenever textbooks are imported
explanation: Article 31 (2) provides the right to compulsory and free education up to the basic level and free education up to the secondary level from the State; clauses (3) and (4) extend free higher education and inclusive education arrangements.

question_text: A municipality bans the use of a local community's language on signboards and in a community-run school, saying uniformity of one national language is required. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The municipality may impose one language for all public purposes
option_b: Every person and community has the right to use their languages and to preserve and promote their language, script, culture and heritage
option_c: Only 'scheduled' languages are protected
option_d: Languages other than the working language may only be used at private homes
explanation: Article 32 (1) gives every person and community the right to use their languages; clause (3) gives every Nepalese community the right to preserve and promote its language, script, culture, civilization and heritage.

question_text: A newly graduated engineer is told by the recruiting office that she must accept a single designated post and has no right to choose among the placements offered. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Any assignment made by the State is binding
option_b: Every citizen has the right to employment and the right to choose employment
option_c: Choice applies only to private-sector jobs
option_d: The right to choose exists only after five years of service
explanation: Article 33 (1) guarantees every citizen the right to employment, with terms, conditions and unemployment benefit as provided for in Federal law; clause (2) expressly recognises the right to choose employment.

question_text: Workers at a garment factory form a union and seek collective bargaining, and the owner responds by dismissing the union leaders. Under the Constitution:
option_a: A labourer's right to form and join trade unions and to engage in collective bargaining is protected
option_b: Trade unions may exist only with the employer's permission
option_c: Collective bargaining is limited to public-sector workers
option_d: Workers may organise but never bargain as a group
explanation: Article 34 (3): 'Every labourer shall have the right to form and join trade unions and to engage in collective bargaining, in accordance with law,' alongside rights to appropriate labour, remuneration, facilities and contributory social security in clauses (1)-(2).

question_text: A hospital refuses to admit a road-accident patient until a large deposit is paid on the spot. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Hospitals may lawfully refuse treatment until payment is assured
option_b: Every citizen has the right to free basic health services and no one shall be deprived of emergency health services
option_c: Emergency care is a courtesy, not a right
option_d: Payment may be demanded whenever beds are limited
explanation: Article 35 (1) provides the right to free basic health services from the State and expressly states that no one shall be deprived of emergency health services; clause (2) protects the right to information about one's medical treatment.

question_text: Following a drought, grain stocks in a district collapse and households are at risk of starvation while traders hold supplies for higher prices. Under the Constitution, citizens of that district:
option_a: Have no claim on the State over food availability
option_b: Have the right to be safe from a state of danger to life from the scarcity of food, and the right to food sovereignty in accordance with law
option_c: May rely only on private charity
option_d: Enjoy food rights only during declared emergencies
explanation: Article 36 (1) establishes the right relating to food; clause (2) guarantees the right to be safe from a state of danger to life from the scarcity of food; clause (3) recognises the right to food sovereignty in accordance with law.

question_text: A municipal office evicts a family from the house they own, after a noise complaint, without any notice, court order or lawful process. Under the Constitution, this is:
option_a: Lawful because the State may relocate anyone for municipal convenience
option_b: Unlawful: no citizen shall be evicted from a residence he or she owns, nor shall it be infringed, except in accordance with law
option_c: Lawful if the eviction is performed during daytime
option_d: Unlawful only if the family has lived there for ten years
explanation: Article 37 (1) gives every citizen the right to appropriate housing; clause (2) provides that no citizen shall be evicted from the residence owned by him or her nor shall his or her residence be infringed except in accordance with law.

question_text: After a divorce, a husband retains exclusive control of the family home and savings, arguing that property acquired during marriage belongs to him alone. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The spouse has an equal right to property and family affairs
option_b: Property acquired during marriage belongs solely to the wage earner
option_c: A wife's rights depend on her husband's consent
option_d: Equal property rights exist only for landless couples
explanation: Article 38 (1) guarantees women equal lineage rights without gender-based discrimination; clause (6) provides that the spouse shall have the equal right to property and family affairs.

question_text: A 13-year-old is taken out of school by her parents and made to work full-time in a brick kiln, then promised in marriage to an older man. Under the Constitution:
option_a: This is permitted as a private family matter
option_b: No child shall be employed in hazardous work such as a mine or factory, no child shall be subjected to child marriage, and such acts are punishable by law with compensation for the child
option_c: Work becomes lawful if the child agrees to it
option_d: Child marriage is allowed with a guardian's consent
explanation: Article 39 (4) bars employment of children in factories, mines or similar hazardous work; clause (5) prohibits child marriage, illegal transport, abduction and hostage-taking; clause (10) makes such acts punishable by law and grants the child compensation.

question_text: A landless Dalit family in Karnali has been farming another's land for decades but is told the State has no programme for them. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The State's obligations to Dalit are limited to reservation in legislatures
option_b: The State shall once provide land to the landless Dalit in accordance with law, besides proportional inclusion, education, health, social security and housing measures
option_c: Dalit rights apply only in urban municipalities
option_d: The State's duty is discharged by its annual budget speech
explanation: Article 40 (1) guarantees proportional inclusion of Dalit; clause (2) free education with scholarship; clause (5) requires the State to once provide land to the landless Dalit in accordance with law; clause (6) requires settlement for Dalit without housing.

question_text: A 78-year-old man is told by an office that the elderly allowance programme does not apply to him because he still lives with relatives. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Senior citizens have the right to special protection and social security from the State
option_b: Elderly benefits depend entirely on each family's income
option_c: The State's duty to senior citizens ends once they have children
option_d: Only institutionalised elderly persons qualify for protection
explanation: Article 41 (1): 'The senior citizens shall have the right to special protection and social security from the State.'

question_text: A citizen who uses a wheelchair is told by a government hospital that its upper floors, counselling rooms and payment counters cannot be reached and no arrangements are planned. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Persons with disabilities have the right to live with dignity and honour and to equal access to public services and facilities
option_b: Accessibility requirements end at the entrance of public buildings
option_c: Equal access is required only in newly built private offices
option_d: A disabled citizen must arrange personal assistance at his or her own cost
explanation: Article 42 (3): 'The citizens with disabilities shall have the right to live with dignity and honour, with the identity of their diversity, and have equal access to public services and facilities.'

question_text: A helpless single mother of three, unable to support or care for the children after her husband's disappearance, is told no support scheme covers her situation. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Social security is a matter of pure executive discretion
option_b: Helpless single women and other indigent, incapacitated and helpless citizens have the right to social security
option_c: Only widows with a death certificate qualify
option_d: Social security is limited to citizens above seventy years of age
explanation: Article 43 (1) confers the right to social security on the indigent, incapacitated and helpless citizens, helpless single women, citizens with disabilities, children, those unable to take care of themselves and citizens of tribes on the verge of extinction.

question_text: A store sells packets of a popular brand of biscuits that turn out to be adulterated, and several buyers fall ill. Under the Constitution:
option_a: Buyers have no claim once the goods are opened
option_b: Every consumer has the right to quality goods and services, and a person injured by substandard goods has the right to obtain compensation in accordance with law
option_c: Compensation is available only if the injury is permanent
option_d: The right to quality goods applies only to imported products
explanation: Article 44 (1) gives every consumer the right to quality goods and services; clause (2) provides that a person who has suffered injury from substandard goods or services has the right to obtain compensation.

question_text: An authority orders a political critic, a Nepali citizen, to leave the country permanently as punishment for his speeches. Under the Constitution, this order is:
option_a: Permitted for reasons of public order
option_b: Unconstitutional, because no citizen shall be exiled
option_c: Allowed if a provincial assembly approves it
option_d: Permitted as part of a foreign-exchange quota
explanation: Article 45 (1) is unqualified: 'No citizen shall be exiled.'

question_text: A citizen whose fundamental right has been violated by a government body wants a binding remedy. Under the Constitution, he or she:
option_a: May only appeal to the legislature through a petition
option_b: Has the right to obtain constitutional remedies in the manner set forth in Article 133 or 144 for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part 3
option_c: Has no remedy short of a new law being enacted
option_d: Must first exhaust arbitration bodies created by the violating agency
explanation: Article 46 (1): 'There shall be a right to obtain constitutional remedies in the manner set forth in Article 133 or 144 for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part' — i.e. the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and allied remedies.

question_text: Years after the Constitution entered into force, certain fundamental rights still have no implementing laws, and officials argue the State may postpone legislation indefinitely. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The State may delay implementation of any right at its pleasure
option_b: The State shall, as required, make legal provisions for implementing the fundamental rights within three years of the commencement of this Constitution
option_c: Implementation laws must be enacted only when the International agencies ask
option_d: The Constitution contains no timeline for fundamental-rights implementation
explanation: Article 47 (1): 'The State shall, as required, make legal provisions for the implementation of the rights conferred by this Part, within three years of the commencement of this Constitution.'

question_text: During a national crisis, the State calls on all citizens for compulsory national service, and a local group urges citizens not to comply while also refusing to protect public property. Which statement aligns with the Constitution?
option_a: Every citizen shall safeguard the nationality, sovereignty and integrity of Nepal, abide by the Constitution and law, and render compulsory service as and when the State so requires
option_b: Duties are voluntary and may be observed selectively
option_c: The duty to abide by law applies only to those in public service
option_d: Compulsory service may never be required of citizens
explanation: Article 48 (1) lists the duties of every citizen, including (a) safeguarding nationality, sovereignty and integrity, (b) abiding by the Constitution and law, (c) rendering compulsory service as and when the State so requires, and further duties to protect public property and common property.

question_text: A provincial minister says the directive principles of the State are 'mere suggestions' that his government may ignore entirely while governing. Under the Constitution, this claim is:
option_a: Correct, because the State may govern however it pleases
option_b: Incorrect: the directive principles, policies and obligations of the State shall be the guiding principles for the governance of the State, and the State shall mobilize means and resources to implement them as required
option_c: Correct, because only courts may enforce these principles through writ petitions
option_d: Correct except during the first five years of a government's term
explanation: Article 49 (1) provides that the directive principles, policies and obligations set forth in Part 4 'shall be the guiding principles for the governance of the State,' and clause (2) requires the State to mobilize means and resources, as required, to implement them.

question_text: A legislator argues that the economic objectives of the State are limited to growing the private business of the wealthy, and that the State has no duty toward egalitarian society. Under the Constitution, the economic objective is to:
option_a: Achieve sustainable economic development through participation and development of public, private and cooperative sectors, leading to a socialism-oriented, independent and self-reliant economy
option_b: Privatize all means of production in favour of a few conglomerates
option_c: Rely exclusively on foreign aid without domestic mobilization
option_d: Keep the economy small so that the State stays simple
explanation: Article 50 (3) states the economic objective of the State: sustainable economic development with rapid growth through maximum mobilization of available means and resources, with participation and development of public, private and cooperative sectors, building a socialism-oriented independent and prosperous economy that is self-reliant and progressive.

question_text: A district official says the State's policies are optional reading, not something citizens may expect the Government to pursue. Under the Constitution, the State shall:
option_a: Ignore its policies unless a private investor funds them
option_b: Have discretion only in times of emergency
option_c: Pursue the policies of the State, which form part of the guiding principles for governance
option_d: Pursue policies only for citizens who pay extra taxes
explanation: Article 51 (1) begins: 'The State shall pursue the following policies' — a long catalogue covering social justice, equality, economic development, education and culture. Read with Article 49, these policies guide, though (per Article 55) they are not directly enforceable in court.

question_text: A commentator claims the State's only obligation is to keep order, and that protecting fundamental rights or building a prosperous nation is beyond its duties. Under the Constitution, it is the obligation of the State to:
option_a: Make Nepal a prosperous and affluent country by protecting and promoting fundamental rights and human rights, pursuing the directive principles and gradually implementing the policies, while keeping intact the freedom, sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence of Nepal
option_b: Do nothing beyond collecting revenue and maintaining police
option_c: Focus solely on international relations, leaving domestic welfare to NGOs
option_d: Guarantee prosperity only for public employees
explanation: Article 52 (1): 'It shall be the obligation of the State to make Nepal a prosperous and affluent country by protecting and promoting fundamental rights and human rights, pursuing directive principles of the State and gradually implementing policies of the State, while keeping intact the freedom, sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence of Nepal.'

question_text: A citizens' group asks how the people will ever know what the Government has done toward the directive principles. The Constitution provides that the Government of Nepal:
option_a: May report only if Parliament insists in writing
option_b: Shall submit an annual report on the steps taken and achievements made in implementing the directive principles, policies and obligations, which the President shall cause to be laid through the Prime Minister before the Federal Parliament
option_c: Must publish such a report in the Gazette without any parliamentary laying
option_d: Has no reporting duty whatsoever in this regard
explanation: Article 53 (1) requires the Government of Nepal to submit an annual report of steps taken and achievements made in the implementation of the directive principles, policies and obligations of the State to the President, who shall cause it to be laid through the Prime Minister before the Federal Parliament.

question_text: A law student asks where within the Federal Parliament the progressive implementation of the directive principles would be reviewed. The Constitution requires:
option_a: A committee in the Federal Parliament, in accordance with law, to monitor and evaluate whether the directive principles, policies and obligations have been implemented progressively
option_b: A private audit firm appointed by the Government itself
option_c: No monitoring at all, since these principles are not binding
option_d: A commission composed exclusively of provincial chief ministers
explanation: Article 54 (1): 'There shall be a committee, in accordance with law, in the Federal Parliament in order to monitor and evaluate whether the directive principles, policies and obligations of the State set forth in this Part have been implemented progressively or not.'

question_text: A citizen files a case in court demanding that judges order the State, by decree, to complete a specific economic policy of Article 51 immediately. Under the Constitution, the court should:
option_a: Order full implementation at once, citing Part 4 as binding law
option_b: Partially order it, since every policy is a constitutional command
option_c: Dismiss the question: no question may be raised in any court as to whether any matter contained in Part 4 has been implemented
option_d: Order implementation but only for citizens residing in municipalities
explanation: Article 55 (1): 'No question shall be raised in any court as to whether any matter contained in this Part has been implemented or not.' The directive principles are guiding and non-justiciable, in contrast to the enforceable fundamental rights of Part 3.

question_text: A provincial minister claims that the Province is fully sovereign and may refuse to follow the Constitution whenever its provincial law says otherwise, and that the local level is merely a department of the Province. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The main structure of the State has three levels — Federation, State and Local — all of which exercise the power of State of Nepal pursuant to the Constitution and law
option_b: The Federation alone holds State power and the other levels are advisory
option_c: Each level is sovereign and may act independently of the Constitution
option_d: The local level is directly subordinate to the Federation, not the Province
explanation: Article 56 (1) fixes the main structure at three levels — the Federation, the State and the Local level; clause (2) provides that all three levels exercise the power of State of Nepal pursuant to this Constitution and law, and clause (6) makes all levels jointly protect the federal democratic republic and its institutions.

question_text: The State Assembly of a province enacts a law on a State-list (Schedule-6) matter that contradicts an existing Federal law on the same subject. What happens under the Constitution?
option_a: The State law prevails over the Federal law within the province
option_b: The State law is invalid to the extent of its inconsistency with the Federal law, because State laws under the concurrent lists must not be inconsistent with Federal law
option_c: A State referendum decides which law operates
option_d: Both laws remain fully valid and courts choose case-by-case
explanation: Article 57 (6) provides that any law made by the State Assembly under the concurrent lists must not be inconsistent with Federal law and that a State law which is inconsistent with the Federal law is invalid to the extent of such inconsistency.

question_text: A field of policy activity appears in none of the Federal list (Schedule-5), State list (Schedule-6), Local list (Schedule-8) or the concurrent lists. Which level of government has power over it?
option_a: The Local level, as the closest to the people
option_b: The State level, by a resolution of all provinces acting jointly
option_c: No level may act until the Constitution is amended
option_d: The Federation, which has power over any matter not enumerated in the Federal, State, Local or Concurrent lists, or not otherwise specified in the Constitution
explanation: Article 58 (1): 'The Federation shall have power on any matter not enumerated in the Federal List, State List, List of Local level or Concurrent List or on any matter which is not so specified in this Constitution as to be exercised by any level.'

question_text: A hydropower dam is built on a river flowing through a district, and the affected local communities say they should receive a share of the benefits. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The Federation, State and Local level shall provide for equitable distribution of benefits derived from natural resources or development, with specified portions distributed by law as royalty, services or goods to project-affected regions and local communities
option_b: All benefits belong solely to the private developer that holds the licence
option_c: Only the Federation and Province receive benefits, never local communities
option_d: Communities receive benefits only if they first made an investment
explanation: Article 59 (4) requires the Federation, State and Local level to provide for equitable distribution of benefits from the use of natural resources or development, distributing certain portions by law as royalty, services or goods to the project-affected regions and local communities; clause (5) requires priority for local-community investment.

question_text: A provincial government asks how much fiscal transfer it should receive from the Centre and on what basis that amount is fixed. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The amount of fiscal transfer receivable by the State and Local level is as recommended by the National Natural Resources and Fiscal Commission, with distribution among the three levels made in a balanced and transparent manner
option_b: The provincial government fixes its own transfer at whatever sum it enacts
option_c: The Federation gives an equal, fixed sum to every province regardless of need
option_d: Transfers depend entirely on a private negotiation with the Centre each year
explanation: Article 60 (2)-(3) require the Government of Nepal to make equitable distribution of collected revenue, with the amount of fiscal transfer receivable by the State and Local level as recommended by the National Natural Resources and Fiscal Commission; clause (7) requires balanced and transparent distribution.

question_text: A citizen asks what the President of Nepal actually is, in constitutional terms. The President is:
option_a: The head of government with executive authority over all ministries
option_b: The head of state of Nepal, whose main duty is to abide by and protect the Constitution and to promote the national unity of Nepal
option_c: A ceremonial figurehead with no duties at all
option_d: The chairperson of the Federal Parliament
explanation: Article 61 (2) makes the President the head of state who performs functions in accordance with the Constitution and Federal law; clause (3) requires the President to promote national unity; clause (4) makes the main duty to abide by and protect the Constitution.

question_text: During a Presidential election, a candidate secures the highest number of votes in the electoral college but less than half the total votes. What happens next under the Constitution?
option_a: That candidate is elected outright as the highest vote-getter
option_b: Voting takes place between the two candidates with the highest votes, and the candidate securing more than fifty percent is elected
option_c: The election is declared void and the Prime Minister nominates the President
option_d: The third-place candidate decides which of the top two wins
explanation: Article 62 (3) requires a majority of the then existing total votes of the electoral college; if none secures a majority, clause (4) provides for a runoff between the top two candidates, with the candidate securing more than fifty percent elected.

question_text: A President's five-year term expires while the country is still preparing for an election of a successor. What happens under the Constitution?
option_a: The office lies vacant and functions are suspended
option_b: The Vice-President automatically begins a fresh five-year term
option_c: The President continues to discharge functions under the Constitution until another elected President assumes office
option_d: The Chief Justice dissolves the office permanently
explanation: Article 63 (1) sets the Presidential term at five years from election; clause (2) provides that a President whose term has expired shall continue to discharge the functions under the Constitution until another elected President assumes office.

question_text: A political party proposes its 50-year-old general secretary, who is qualified for the Federal Parliament, as Presidential candidate — but the same person has already been elected President twice. Under the Constitution:
option_a: He may stand because only three prior terms are disqualifying
option_b: He is qualified, since he meets the age and Federal Parliament qualification requirements
option_c: He is disqualified, because a person who has already been elected twice as the President cannot become a candidate again
option_d: He must first resign from his party before being considered
explanation: Article 64 (1) requires qualification to become a member of the Federal Parliament, age of at least forty-five years, and no disqualification by law; clause (2) adds that a person already elected twice as President cannot become a candidate in the election to the President.

question_text: A student reads that a President can leave office mid-term. Which of the following is NOT a way the Presidential office becomes vacant under the Constitution?
option_a: The President tenders resignation in writing to the Vice-President
option_b: A motion of impeachment against the President is passed under Article 101
option_c: The Prime Minister orders the President to step down by majority decision
option_d: The term of office expires or the President dies
explanation: Article 65 (1) exhaustively lists the circumstances of vacancy: resignation in writing to the Vice-President, impeachment passed under Article 101, expiry of term, or death. A Prime Minister's order is not among them.

question_text: The President wishes to issue an executive decision in an area where the Constitution does not specially require a particular body's recommendation. How must this be done?
option_a: On the recommendation and with the consent of the Council of Ministers, submitted through the Prime Minister
option_b: On the President's sole discretion without any consultation
option_c: On the recommendation of the Chief Justice alone
option_d: After a resolution of the Federal Parliament
explanation: Article 66 (2): in exercising powers under the Constitution or a Federal law, the President performs all functions on the recommendation and with the consent of the Council of Ministers, except where a specific body or official is designated; such recommendation and consent are submitted through the Prime Minister.

question_text: The President leaves the country for a medical treatment abroad. Who performs the functions of the President during this absence?
option_a: The Prime Minister automatically
option_b: The Vice-President
option_c: The Speaker of the House of Representatives
option_d: The Chief Justice temporarily assumes both roles
explanation: Article 67 (2): 'The functions to be performed by the President shall be performed by the Vice-president during the absence of the President.'

question_text: The Vice-President wants to step down early. To whom must the Vice-President tender resignation in writing to validly vacate the office?
option_a: The Prime Minister
option_b: The Speaker
option_c: The President
option_d: The Chief Justice
explanation: Article 68 (1) lists the circumstances of vacancy of the Vice-Presidential office, beginning with resignation tendered in writing to the President, alongside impeachment under Article 101, expiry of term, or death.

question_text: A constitution expert is asked what rules govern the Vice-President's qualifications and selection. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The Vice-President is appointed by the Prime Minister and needs no qualification
option_b: Provisions relating to the qualification, procedures of election and term of office of the Vice-President shall be the same as that of the President
option_c: The Vice-President is elected by the State Assemblies alone
option_d: The Vice-President serves for life
explanation: Article 69 (1): 'Provisions relating to the qualification, procedures of election and term of office of the Vice-President shall be the same as that of the President.'

question_text: In the same electoral cycle, both the President and the Vice-President turn out to be middle-aged men of the same ethnic community. Under the Constitution, this is:
option_a: Permissible, since the Constitution prescribes no composition rule
option_b: Permissible if both receive a majority of votes
option_c: Contrary to the Constitution: election to the President and the Vice-President shall be made so as to have representation of different sex or community
option_d: Contrary to the Constitution only if a national census objects
explanation: Article 70 (1): 'Election to the President and the Vice-president under this Constitution shall be so made as to have representation of different sex or community.'

question_text: A newly elected President is about to assume office and asks before whom the oath of office and secrecy is to be taken. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The Chief Justice
option_b: The Prime Minister
option_c: The Speaker
option_d: The Vice-President-elect
explanation: Article 71 (1): the President takes an oath of office and secrecy before the Chief Justice, and the Vice-President before the President, as provided for in the Federal law.

question_text: The President asks how the remuneration and facilities of the office are set. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The President fixes his or her own salary by decree
option_b: They are as provided for in the Federal Act, and as specified by the Government of Nepal until such Act is made
option_c: They are fixed by a constitutional amendment each year
option_d: They are determined by provincial assemblies jointly
explanation: Article 72 (1): 'The remuneration and other facilities of the President and the Vice-president shall be as provided for in the Federal Act, and as specified by the Government of Nepal until such Act is made.'

question_text: A parliamentarian moves that the President and the Vice-President should share a single secretariat to cut costs. Under the Constitution, the correct position is:
option_a: There shall be separate offices for the performance of the functions of the President and the Vice-President
option_b: They may share one office whenever ministers agree
option_c: A single office is required to ensure coordination
option_d: Both offices must be located inside the Parliament building
explanation: Article 73 (1) requires separate offices for the performance of the functions of the President and the Vice-President, and clause (2) requires the Government of Nepal to arrange employees and other provisions for those offices.

question_text: A foreign visitor asks what form of government the Constitution of Nepal establishes. Under the Constitution, the form of government is:
option_a: A monarchy with a ceremonial council
option_b: A presidential system in which the President holds all executive power
option_c: Multi-party, competitive, federal, democratic, republican, parliamentary form of government based on pluralism
option_d: A single-party state governed by a revolutionary committee
explanation: Article 74 (1): 'The form of government of Nepal shall be multi-party, competitive, federal, democratic, republican, parliamentary form of government based on pluralism.'

question_text: A minister claims that all executive authority belongs personally to the Prime Minister, who may govern without collective decision-making. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The Prime Minister alone holds and exercises the entire executive power
option_b: Executive power is vested in the Council of Ministers, and all Federal executive functions are performed in the name of the Government of Nepal
option_c: The President exercises all executive power on behalf of the nation
option_d: Executive power is shared between the Chief Justice and the Prime Minister
explanation: Article 75 (1) vests the executive power of Nepal in the Council of Ministers; clause (2) places the responsibility for issuing general directives and controlling and regulating governance on the Council of Ministers; clause (3) requires Federal executive functions to be performed in the name of the Government of Nepal.

question_text: After a general election, no single party commands a clear majority in the House of Representatives. What is the constitutional path to forming a government?
option_a: The President must appoint the candidate of the largest party without further ado
option_b: The President appoints as Prime Minister a member of the House of Representatives who can command a majority with the support of two or more parties
option_c: The House is dissolved immediately and fresh elections are declared
option_d: The President asks the Supreme Court to nominate a caretaker Prime Minister
explanation: Article 76 (2) provides that where no party has a clear majority, the President shall appoint as Prime Minister a member of the House of Representatives who can command a majority with the support of two or more parties; clauses (3)-(8) then set out the thirty-day confidence rules and fallback to the largest party, culminating in dissolution where no government can be formed.

question_text: A newly formed coalition Prime Minister is asked how quickly the government must prove its support in the House of Representatives. Under the Constitution:
option_a: A vote of confidence must be obtained no later than thirty days after the date of appointment
option_b: A vote of confidence is required only at the next general election
option_c: The Prime Minister may rule for a full term without any confidence vote
option_d: Confidence is presumed until a no-confidence motion is twice filed
explanation: Article 76 (4): 'The Prime Minister appointed under clause (2) or (3) shall obtain a vote of confidence from the House of Representatives no later than thirty days after the date of such appointment.'

question_text: A Prime Minister chosen as the leader of the largest party fails to secure a vote of confidence, and no coalition alternative can be formed. What does the Constitution then direct?
option_a: The President appoints a fresh caretaker for a fixed two-year term
option_b: The President, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, dissolves the House of Representatives and sets an election to be completed within six months
option_c: The Chief Justice temporarily assumes the office of Prime Minister
option_d: The House is suspended indefinitely until parties reconcile
explanation: Article 76 (7): where the Prime Minister appointed under clause (6) fails to obtain a vote of confidence or no Prime Minister can be appointed, the President shall, on recommendation of the Prime Minister, dissolve the House of Representatives and appoint a date of election so that the election to another House of Representatives is completed within six months.

question_text: The leader of a parliamentary party that commands a majority loses the support of his own party and quit his post. While a successor is being formed, what happens to the outgoing Council of Ministers?
option_a: It shall continue to act until another Council of Ministers is constituted
option_b: It is immediately suspended and the President alone governs
option_c: All ministers are automatically reappointed indefinitely
option_d: The Council dissolves and the provinces take over Federal work
explanation: Article 77 (1) sets out the circumstances in which the office of the Prime Minister falls vacant; clause (3) provides that if the office of the Prime Minister falls vacant, the same Council of Ministers shall continue to act until another Council of Ministers is constituted.

question_text: The Prime Minister recommends a well-known economist who is not a member of the Federal Parliament to become a Minister. Under the Constitution, this is:
option_a: Impermissible, because only sitting members can ever be Ministers
option_b: Permissible on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, provided the appointee obtains membership of the Federal Parliament within six months of taking oath
option_c: Permissible only if the Supreme Court approves the nomination
option_d: Permissible, but the appointee may serve the full term without Parliament membership
explanation: Article 78 (1) allows the President, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, to appoint a person who is not a member of the Federal Parliament as a Minister; clause (2) requires that Minister to obtain membership of the Federal Parliament within six months from the date of taking oath; clause (4) disqualifies anyone defeated in the election to the then House.

question_text: A new Prime Minister asks before whom the oath of office and secrecy is to be taken. Under the Constitution:
option_a: The Chief Justice, acting as the senior-most constitutional officer
option_b: The President
option_c: The Speaker of the House of Representatives
option_d: The Vice-President
explanation: Article 80 (1): the Prime Minister, Deputy Prime Minister and Ministers take an oath of office and secrecy before the President, while Ministers of State and Assistant Ministers take it before the Prime Minister.

question_text: The President asks to be kept informed of the Government's key decisions and the state of the country. Under the Constitution, the Prime Minister shall inform the President about:
option_a: Nothing; the Government is answerable only to the House of Representatives
option_b: Only Bills when they have been passed, not before introduction
option_c: Resolutions of the Council of Ministers, Bills to be introduced in the Federal Parliament, necessary information commanded by the President on those matters, and the current general state of the country's affairs and foreign relations
option_d: Only matters concerning foreign relations
explanation: Article 81 (1) requires the Prime Minister to inform the President about (a) resolutions of the Council of Ministers, (b) Bills to be introduced in the Federal Parliament, (c) other necessary information the President commands on those matters, and (d) the current general state of affairs of the country and matters concerning foreign relations.

question_text: A litigant challenges a government decision in court solely on the ground that the internal rules for transacting government business were not followed. Under the Constitution, the court should:
option_a: Overturn the decision, because procedural rules are justiciable
option_b: Not entertain the challenge: no question may be raised in any court as to whether the rules approved by the Government for transacting its business have been observed
option_c: Order a full inquiry into the internal minutes of the Cabinet
option_d: Require the Cabinet to redraft its rules before proceeding
explanation: Article 82 (1) allocates the business of the Government of Nepal in accordance with rules approved by the Government; clause (2) provides that no question may be raised in any court as to whether such rules have been observed — an internal-machinery rule, in contrast to the ordinary grounds for judicial review.
